lead: MISRA C is a coding standard that removes risky C constructs—recursion, hidden conversions, pointer arithmetic outside arrays—so embedded software behaves predictably. ISO 26262 is a functional-safety standard: it starts from a hazard, assigns an ASIL level from severity, exposure and controllability, then demands documented evidence across a safety lifecycle. Suppliers use both together: MISRA keeps the code clean, ISO 26262 proves the item is safe enough. Only a few universities teach this material in depth.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.2 for how ECUs exchange safety-relevant frames, and Chapter 6.4 for diagnostic monitors that feed fault detection.

blocks.text: MISRA C is a coding standard for C in embedded systems. MISRA C:2012 classifies each guideline as mandatory, required or advisory. A required guideline must be followed or formally deviated; a deviation is a written permit with justification and risk analysis, not a silent exception.

The rules remove risky constructs. Common rules: no recursion; no use of the dynamic memory allocation and deallocation functions (malloc, calloc, realloc, free) at all; no implicit conversion that loses a value; braces on every if and else body; no pointer arithmetic outside an array; and check every return value that reports an error. If a project needs a one-off start-up allocation, that is a documented deviation, not a MISRA rule. MISRA also limits features that are hard to analyse statically, such as macros with side effects.

A static-analysis tool checks the source. The team fixes each violation or records a deviation. Passing MISRA gives disciplined code, not proof of functional safety. Generated code must pass the same checks or the generator must be qualified.

sections.h3: ISO 26262: hazard to ASIL to evidence

blocks.text: ISO 26262:2018 is the functional-safety standard for road vehicles. It has parts 1–12 and follows a V-model: requirements, implementation, then verification. Part 3 is the concept phase; part 6 covers software.

The item definition fixes the boundary: which ECUs, sensors, actuators and functions are inside. HARA (hazard analysis and risk assessment) studies each hazardous event. It rates severity S0–S3, exposure E0–E4 and controllability C0–C3. The combination gives an ASIL: A, B, C or D, with D the highest, or QM when no safety requirement applies.

Each hazardous event produces a safety goal, such as 'no unintended full braking at speed'. The safety goal inherits the ASIL. The technical safety concept names safety mechanisms: plausibility checks, watchdog timers, redundant sensors and safe states. ASIL decomposition can split a requirement into two independent lower-ASIL requirements, but independence must be demonstrated.

The fault tolerant time interval (FTTI) is the minimum time from the occurrence of a fault to the possible occurrence of a hazardous event. The safety mechanism must detect the fault and finish the safe reaction inside that interval. Detection budget = FTTI − sensor sampling − confirmation − actuator.

Hardware metrics judge the architecture using failure rates and diagnostic coverage. SPFM = 1 − (λ<sub>SPF</sub> + λ<sub>RF</sub>)/λ<sub>total</sub>, where λ<sub>SPF</sub> is single-point fault rate, λ<sub>RF</sub> residual fault rate, λ<sub>total</sub> total failure rate; the diagnostic coverage of each safety mechanism is an input to these numbers. LFM judges how well latent (hidden) faults are covered. Verification includes tests, fault injection and independent assessment. MISRA supports the software part, but it does not replace HARA or metrics.

examples.question: A safety goal has FTTI = 200 ms. Sensor sampling takes 20 ms, two-frame confirmation takes 40 ms, and the actuator needs 30 ms. Find the time left for fault detection.
steps: Write the budget: detection time = FTTI − sampling − confirmation − actuation.
examples.answer: The detection logic has 110 ms after sampling and confirmation, so the fault must be flagged by 20 + 40 + 110 = 170 ms after it occurs; the actuator then brings the item to the safe state by 200 ms.
examples.check:
ftti_ms = 200
sampling_ms = 20
confirmation_ms = 40
actuator_ms = 30
detection_ms = ftti_ms - sampling_ms - confirmation_ms - actuator_ms
print(detection_ms)

traps: Passing MISRA checks proves ISO 26262 compliance — false; MISRA is coding evidence only.
ASIL D is the highest integrity level, not a component grade you can buy.
FTTI is not the same as detection time; it includes sensing, confirmation and actuation.
ASIL decomposition does not lower the safety goal; it splits it into independent requirements.
QM is not ASIL 0; it means quality management with no ASIL safety requirement.

quiz.a: A documented permit to break a required guideline, with justification and risk analysis.

quiz.q: Why does MISRA C ban recursion?
quiz.a: Stack depth becomes hard to bound, so worst-case memory use cannot be proved.

quiz.q: An FTTI is 150 ms. Sampling is 10 ms, confirmation is 20 ms, actuator is 20 ms. Find the detection budget.
A team passes MISRA but has no HARA. Can it claim ASIL B compliance?
quiz.a: No. MISRA is coding evidence only; ASIL B also needs HARA, safety goals, technical concept and confirmation measures.
ASIL D is the highest safety integrity level; QM means normal quality management with no ASIL requirement.

quiz.q: An ASIL D safety requirement is split into two requirements. What ASILs may they take, and what must be shown?
quiz.a: ASIL B(D) + ASIL B(D), or ASIL C(D) + ASIL A(D); the two must be sufficiently independent, each keeps the D tag, and together they must meet the original ASIL D requirement.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, teams use static analysers with MISRA rule sets and keep a traceable safety case in requirements tools. ISO 21448 (SOTIF) extends safety thinking to performance limits of sensors and ADAS. Search for 'MISRA C:2012 Amendment 2', 'ISO 26262-6 software', 'ASIL decomposition' and 'SPFM LFM calculation'.
